[[File:Phalaris arundinacea NP.JPG|thumb|[[Variegation|Variegated form]], garden of Islington College, [[Nepal]]]]

'''''Phalaris arundinacea''''', or '''reed canary grass''',<ref>{{cite book |editor1-last=Lee |editor1-first=Sangtae |editor2-last=Chang |editor2-first=Kae Sun |title=English Names for Korean Native Plants |year=2015 |publisher=[[Korea National Arboretum]] |location=Pocheon |isbn=978-89-97450-98-5 |page=568 |url=http://www.forest.go.kr/kna/special/download/English_Names_for_Korean_Native_Plants.pdf |access-date=12 March 2019 |via=[[Korea Forest Service]]}}</ref> is a tall, [[Perennial plant|perennial]] grass that commonly forms extensive single-species stands along the margins of lakes and streams and in wet open areas, with a wide distribution in [[Europe]], [[Asia]], northern [[Africa]] and [[North America]].<ref name=grin>{{GRIN | access-date = 2017-12-15}}</ref> Other common names for the plant include '''gardener's-garters''' and '''ribbon grass''' in [[English language|English]], '''{{Lang|fr|alpiste roseau}}''' in [[French language|French]], '''{{Lang|de|Rohrglanzgras}}''' in [[German language|German]], '''{{Lang|ja-Latn|kusa-yoshi}}''' in [[Japanese language|Japanese]], '''{{Lang|pt|caniço-malhado}}''' in [[Portuguese language|Portuguese]], and '''{{Lang|es|hierba cinta}}''' and '''{{Lang|es|pasto cinto}}''' in [[Spanish language|Spanish]].<ref name=usda>[https://plants.usda.gov/plantguide/pdf/pg_phar3.pdf ''Phalaris arundinacea''.] USDA NRCS Plant Guide.</ref>

==Description==
The stems can reach {{convert|2|metres|ft}} in height.<ref name=fs>{{Cite web|last=Waggy|first=Melissa, A.|year=2010|url=http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/graminoid/phaaru/all.html|title=''Phalaris arundinacea''|website=Fire Effects Information System. U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Research Station, Fire Sciences Laboratory}}</ref> The [[leaf]] blades are usually green, but may be [[variegated]]. The [[panicle]]s are up to {{Convert|30|cm}} long.<ref name=fs/> The spikelets are light green, often streaked with darker green or purple.<ref name=china>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200025869 ''Phalaris arundinacea''.] Flora of China.</ref> This is a perennial grass which spreads underground by its thick [[rhizomes]].<ref name=fs/>

==Uses==
A number of [[cultivars]] of ''P. arundinacea'' have been selected for use as [[ornamental plant]]s, including variegated (striped) cultivars – sometimes called '''ribbon grass''' – such as 'Castor' and 'Feesey'. The latter has a pink tinge to the leaves.<ref name=mobot>[http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/gardens-gardening/your-garden/plant-finder/plant-details/kc/t250/phalaris-arundinacea-var.-picta-feesey.aspx ''Phalaris arundinacea'' var. ''picta'' 'Feesey'.]</ref> When grown, although drought-tolerant, it likes abundant water and can even be grown as an aquatic plant.<ref name=mobot/>

Reed canary grass grows well on poor soil and contaminated industrial sites. Researchers at [[Teesside University]]'s Contaminated Land & Water Centre have suggested it is ideal for [[phytoremediation]], which improves [[soil quality]] and biodiversity at [[brownfield land|brownfield]] sites.{{citation needed|date=June 2012}}

The grass can also easily be turned into bricks or pellets for burning in [[biomass (energy)|biomass]] power stations.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Bond|first1=Sam|title=Candidate crops for contaminated land biofuels crop considered|website=edie.net/crc|url=http://www.edie.net/news/news_story.asp?id=17706&channel=0|date=2010-02-23|access-date=2010-04-17}}</ref> Furthermore, it provides fibers which find use in pulp and papermaking processes.<ref name=anders>Andersson, B. and E. Lindvall. [http://www.internationalgrasslands.org/files/igc/publications/1997/1-03-003.pdf Use of biomass from reed canary grass (''Phalaris arundinacea'') as raw material for production of paper pulp and fuel.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304125553/http://www.internationalgrasslands.org/files/igc/publications/1997/1-03-003.pdf |date=2016-03-04 }} internationalgrasslands.org.</ref>

''P. arundinacea'' is also planted as a [[hay]] crop or for [[forage]].

This species of ''Phalaris'' may also be used as a source of the psychedelic drugs [[Dimethyltryptamine|DMT]], [[5-MeO-DMT]] and [[Bufotenin|5-OH-DMT]] (bufotenin), as well as [[Hordenine]] and [[5-MeO-NMT]];<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Wilkinson|first1=S.|title=428. 5-Methoxy-N-methyltryptamine: a new indole alkaloid from Phalaris arundinacea L|journal=Journal of the Chemical Society (Resumed)|date=1958|page=2079|doi=10.1039/jr9580002079}}</ref> however, N,N-DMT is considered most desirable. Although the concentrations of these compounds are lower than in other potential sources, such as ''[[Psychotria viridis]]'' and ''[[Mimosa tenuiflora]]'', large enough quantities of the grass can be refined to make an ad hoc [[ayahuasca]] brew.

==Ecology==
In many places, ''P. arundinacea'' is an [[invasive species]] in [[wetland]]s, particularly in disturbed areas.<ref name="Apfelbaum">{{cite journal|last1=Apfelbaum|first1=Stephen I.|last2=Sams|first2=Charles E.|year=1997|title=Ecology and control of reed canary grass (''Phalaris arundinacea L.'')|journal=Natural Areas Journal|volume=7|issue=2|pages=69–74|jstor=43910930}}</ref> It has been reported as an invasive weed in [[floodplain]]s, riverside [[meadow]]s, and other wetland habitats around the world. When ''P. arundinacea'' invades a wetland, it inhibits native vegetation and reduces [[biological diversity]].<ref name=kim>Kim, K. D., et al. (2006). Controlling ''Phalaris arundinacea'' (reed canarygrass) with live willow stakes: A density-dependent response. ''Ecological Engineering'' '''26''' pp. 219–227. {{DOI|10.1016/j.ecoleng.2006.02.007}}.</ref> It alters the entire [[ecosystem]].<ref name=lav>Lavergne, S. and J. Molofsky. (2004). Reed canary grass (''Phalaris arundinacea'') as a biological model in the study of plant invasions. ''Critical Reviews in Plant Sciences'' 23(5) 415–429. {{DOI|10.1080/07352680490505934}}.</ref> The grass propagates by seed and rhizome,<ref name="Apfelbaum"/> and once established, is difficult to eradicate.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Batzer|first1=Darold P.|last2=Sharitz|first2=Rebecca R.|year=2006|chapter=Wetland Restoration|title=Ecology of freshwater and estuarine wetlands|location=Berkeley, California|publisher=University of California Press|page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=aEzkrNYyI-4C&pg=PA395 395]|isbn=978-0-520-24777-2}}</ref>

==Distribution==
''P. arundinacea'' now has a worldwide distribution. While it is generally considered to be native to both North America and Eurasia, this is a matter of debate. It appears that the North American populations are a mixture of introduced European cultivars and indigenous varieties.<ref name = CABI>{{cite journal | url = https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/55423#todistribution | title = ''Phalaris arundinacea'' (reed canary grass) | work = CABI Compendium | date = 2019 | volume = CABI Compendium | access-date = 16 March 2020 | publisher = CABI| doi = 10.1079/cabicompendium.55423 | doi-access = free }} ''citing, inter alia,'' {{Cite book|author1=Häfliger, Ernst |author2=Scholz, Hildemar |year=1980 |title=Grass weeds / 2, Weeds of the subfamilies 'Chloridoideae', 'Pooideae', 'Oryzoideae' |series=Documenta |location=Basel, Switzerland |publisher=CIBA-Geigy }}</ref>

==Chemical properties==
Specimens contain varying levels of [[hordenine]] and [[gramine]].<ref>{{Cite journal|author1=Woods, D. L. |author2=Hovin, A. W.  |author3=Marten, G. C.  |year=1979 |title=Seasonal Variation of Hordenine and Gramine Concentrations and Their Heritability in Reed Canarygrass |journal=Crop Science |volume=19 |issue=6 |pages=853–857 |doi=10.2135/cropsci1979.0011183X001900060026x }}</ref>

Leaves of ''P. arundinacea'' contain [[Dimethyltryptamine|DMT]], [[5-MeO-DMT]] and related compounds.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Pennanen |first=Petrus |date=December 1995 |title=Tryptamine Carriers |url=http://www.deoxy.org/trypfaq.htm#67 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19970706115948/http://www.deoxy.org/trypfaq.htm#67 |archive-date=6 July 1997 |url-status=usurped }} ''citing'' {{Cite journal|last=Smith |first=Terence A. |year=1977 |title=Review: Tryptamine and Related Compounds in Plants |journal=Phytochemistry |volume=16 |pages=171–175 |doi=10.1016/S0031-9422(00)86778-3 }}</ref> Levels of [[beta-carboline]]s<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Marten |first1=G. C. |last2=Jordan |first2=R. M. |last3=Hovin |first3=A. W. |year=1976 |title=Biological Significance of Reed Canarygrass Alkaloids and Associated Palatability Variation to Grazing Sheep and Cattle |journal=Agronomy Journal |volume=68 |issue=6 |pages=909–914 |doi=10.2134/agronj1976.00021962006800060017x |bibcode=1976AgrJ...68..909M }}</ref> and [[hordenine]]<ref>{{Cite book |last=Saxton |first=J. Edwin |display-authors=etal |year=1974 |title=The alkaloids Volume 4, A review of the literature published between July 1972 and June 1973 |series=(Specialist Periodical Reports) |publisher=The Chemical Society |location=London |isbn=978-0-85186-287-3 |page=130 }}</ref> have also been reported.
